Wealth in A Cold Climate

Wealth in A Cold Climate

Latitude is crucial to a nation's economic strength.

{drop:14} A Dr William Masters was reading a mosquitæs when inspiration struck. "There was this anecdote about the great yellow-fever epidemic that hit Philadelphia in 1793," Masters recalls. "This epidemic decimated the city until the first frost came." The inclement weather froze out the insects, allowing Philadelphia to

{drop:15} B If weather could the key to a city's fortunes. Masters thought, then why not to the historical fortunes of nations? And could frost lie at the heart of one of the most enduring economic mysteries of all—why are almost all the wealthy, industrialised nations to be found at latitudes above 40 degrees? After two years of research, he thinks that he has found a piece of the puzzle. Masters, an agricultural economist from Purdue University in Indiana, and Margaret McMillan at Tufts University, Boston, show that annual frosts are among the factors that distinguish rich nations from ones. Their study is published this month in the Joumal of Economic Growth. The pair that cold snaps have two main benefits—they freeze that would otherwise destroy crops, and also freeze organisms, such as rncE.quitc— that carry disease. The result is agricultural abundance and a big workforce.

{drop:16} C The academics two sets of information. The first was average income for countries, the second climate data from the University of East Anglia. They found a curious tally between the sets. Countries having five or more frosty days a month are uniformly rich, those with fewer than five are impoverished. The authors speculate that tie five-day figure is imcxrtant; it could be the minimum time needed to kill pests in the soil. Masters says: "For example, Finland is a small country that is growing quickly, but Bolivia is a small country that isn't growing at all. Perhaps climate has something to do with that." In fact, limited frosts bring huge benefits to farmers. The chills kill insects or render them inactive; cold weather slows the break-up of plant and animal material in the soil, allowing it to become richer; and frosts ensure a build-up of moisture in the ground for spring, reducing dependence on seasonal rains. There are exceptions to the "cold equals rich" argument. There are well-heeled tropiczl places such as Hong Kong and Singapore, a result of their superior trading positions. Likewise, not all European countries are moneyed—in the former communist colonies, economic potential was by politics.

{drop:17} D Masters stresses that climate will never be the overriding factor—the wealth of nations is too complicated to be attributable to just one factor. Climate, he feels, somehow combines with other factors—such as the presence of institutions, including govemments, and access to

42 trading routes—to determine whether a country will do well. Traditionally, Masters says, economists thought that institutions had the biggest effect on the economy, they brought order to a country in the form of, for example, laws and property rights. With order, so the thinking went, affluence. "But there are sorne problems that even countries with institutions have not been able to get around," he says. "My feeling is that, as countries get richer, they get better institutions. And the accumulation of wealth and improvement in governing institutions are both helped by a favourable environment, including climate."

{drop:18} E This dæs not mean, he insists, that tropical c:ountries are economic help and to remain penniless. Instead, richer countries should change the way in which foreign aid is given. Instead of aid geared towards improving govemance, it should on technology to improve agriculture and to combat disease. Masters cites one example: "There are regions in India that have with irrigation—agricultural prcxiuctivity has gone up and there has been an improvement in health." Supplying vaccines against tropical diseases and developing varieties that grow in the tropics would break the gxwerty cycle.

{drop:19} F Other minds have applied themselves to the split between poor and rich nations, citing anthroclimatic and reasons for why nations are the most affluent. In 350BC, Aristotle observed that "those who live in a cold climate...are full of spirit". Jared Diamond, from the University of Califomia at Los Angeles, pointed out in his book Guns, Germs and Steel that Eurasia is broadly aligned east-west, while Africa and the Americzs are aligned north-south. So, in Europe, crops can spread quickly across latitudes climates are similar. One of the first crops, einkom wheat, spread quickly from the Middle East into Europe; it twice as long for com to spread from Mexico to what is now the eastem United States. This easy movement along similar latitudes in Eurasia would also have meant a faster dissemination of other such as the wheel and writing, Diamond speculates. The region also boasted domesticated livestock, which could provide meat, wool and motive in the fields. Blessed with such natural advantages. Eurasia was to take off economically.

{drop:20} G John Gallup and Jeffrey Sachs, two US economists, have also pointed out striking correlations between the geographical location of countries and their wealth. They note that tropical countries between 23.45 degrees north and south of the equator are nearly all pcx)r. In an article for the Harvard Intemational Review, they that "development surely seems to favour the temperate-zone economies, especially those in the northem hemisphere, and those that have managed to avoid both sæialism and the ravages of war. But Masters cautions against geographical determinism, the idea that tropical countries are beyond hope: "Human health and agriculture can be made better through scientific and technological research," he says, -so we shouldn't be writing off these countries. Take Singapore: without air conditioning, it wouldn't rich."

Musical Maladies

Musical Maladies

Norman M. reviews the latest work of Oliver Sacks on music. Music and the brain are both endlessly fascinating subjects, and as a neur(ßcientist ing in auditory learning and memory, I find them intriguing. So I had high expectations of Musicophilia, the latest offering from neurologist and prolific author Oliver Sacks. And to feeling a little guilty reporting that my reactions to the txx»k are mixed. Sacks himself is the part of Musicophilia. He richly his own life in the and reveals highly experiences. The photograph of him on the cover of the tx»ok— which shows him wearing headphones, eyes closed, clearly enchanted as he listens to Alfred Brendel perform Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata—makes a impression that is out by the contents of the Sacks's voice throughout is steady and erudite but never 1 tifical. He is neither self-conscious nor self-promoting. Ille preface gives a gocxl of what the Emk will deliver. In it Sacks explains that he wants to convey the insights gleaned from the "enormous and rapidly growing body of work on the 1 neural underpinnings of musical and imagery, and the complex and often bizarre disorders to which these are prone." He also stresses the importance of "the simple art of observation" and "the richnes of the human context." He wants to combine and description with the latest in technolow," he says, and to imaginatively enter into the rience Of his patients and subjects. The reader can see that Sacks, who has been practicing neurolow for 40 years, is torn between the "old-fashioned" path of observation and the newfangled, high-tech approach: He knows that he needs to take of the latter, but his heart lies with the former. The consists mainly of detailed descriptions of cases, most of them involving patients whom Sacks has seen in his practice. Brief discussions of contemrx»rary neuroscientific rQrts are sprinkled throughout the text. Part I, "Haunted by Music," tEgins with the strange case of Tony Cicoria, a nonmusical, middle-aged who was consumed by a love of music after being hit by lightning. He suddenly to crave listening to piano music, which he had never cared for in the past. He started to play the piano and then to cornlXße music, which arose slx»ntaneously in his mind in a "torrent" of notes. How could this hamxm? Was the psychological? (He had had a near-death experience when the lightning struck him.) Or was it the direct rßult of a change in the auditory regions of his cerebral cortex? Electroencephalography (EEG) showtxl his brain waves to normal in the just after his trauma and subsequent "conversion" to music. 'lhere are now more sensitive tests, but Cicx»ria has declined to undergo them; he does not want to delve into the causes of his musicality. What a shame! Part 11, "A Range of Musicality," covers a wider variety of topics, but unfortunately, some of the chapters offer little or nothing that is new. For example, chapter 13, which is five pag€S 1 long, merely notes that the blind often have better hearing than the sighted. The most interesting chapters are those that present the strangest cases. Chapter 8 is atx»ut "amusia," an inability to hear sounds as music, and "dysharmonia," a highly specific impairment of the ability to hear harmony, with the ability to understand melody left intact. Such "disscx:iations" are found throughout the Sacks recounts. To Sacks's credit, part Ill, "Memory, Movement and Music," brings us into the underappreciated realm of music therapy. Chapter 16 explains how "melodic intonation therapy" is being used to help expressive aphasic patients (those unable to express their thoughts verbally following a stroke or other cerebral incident) once again become capable of fluent In chapter 20, Sacks demonstrates the near-miraculous power of music to animate Parkinson's patients and other with severe movement disorders, even those who are frozen into odd Scientists cannot yet explain how music achieves this effect. TO readers who are unfamiliar with neuroscience and music behavior, Musicophilia may something of a revelation. But the bCX)k will not satisfy thcse seeking the causes and implications of the phenomena Sacks For one thing, Sacks appears to more at ease discussing patients than discussing experiments. And he tends to be rather uncritical in accepting scientific findings and theories. It's true that the causes of music-brain cxidities remain poorly However, Sacks cx»uld have done more to draw out some of the implications of the careful observations that he and other neurologists have made and of the treatments that have been successful. For example, he might have noted that the many specific dissociations among components of music comprehension, such as loss of the ability to perceive harmony but not melody, indicate that there is no music center in the brain. Because many who read the are likely to in the brain Icx:alisation of all mental functions, this was a missed educational oppor-

Another conclusion one could draw is that there to no "cures" for neurological problems involving music. A drug can alleviate a symptom in one patient and aggravate it in another, or can have IX)th and negative effects in the same patient. Treatments mentioned seem to be almost exclusively antiepileptic medications, which "damp down" the excitability of the brain in general; their effectiveness varies widely.
